title: A Meta-Analytic Review of Experiments Examining the Effects of Extrinsic Rewards on Intrinsic Motivation
license: Copyright holder's terms. Linked, not reproduced.

verified.evidence: Title, authors, journal, volume, issue, pages and year matched in search results (APA/Psychological Bulletin listing and university-hosted copies at ubalt.edu, washington.edu, colorado.edu); the results describe a meta-analysis of 128 studies written in response to Cameron & Pierce (1994). DOI follows the APA pattern for this article and was not separately displayed.

summary: A meta-analysis of 128 laboratory experiments on whether rewards reduce people’s later, freely chosen engagement in an interesting task. The authors conclude that expected, tangible rewards made contingent on doing the task reliably undermine intrinsic motivation, while positive verbal feedback tends to enhance it. They interpret the pattern through cognitive evaluation theory: rewards experienced as controlling reduce felt autonomy; rewards experienced as information about competence do not.
arguments: Expected tangible rewards contingent on engagement, completion or performance undermine free-choice intrinsic motivation for interesting tasks.
Verbal rewards (positive feedback) tend to enhance intrinsic motivation, especially for adults.
Whether a reward is felt as controlling or as informational is the moderating mechanism.
The paper rebuts an earlier meta-analysis (Cameron & Pierce, 1994) that reached a more benign conclusion.
design: Meta-analysis of 128 experiments, mostly laboratory studies with student participants and interesting tasks.
strengths: Large, systematic synthesis; separates reward types and contingencies rather than asking whether “rewards” in general help or hurt.
limitations: Mostly short laboratory sessions with tasks chosen to be interesting; the outcome is minutes of free-choice play, not job performance. Generalization to paid work, where pay is expected and necessary, is indirect.
contested: Cameron, Pierce and colleagues disputed the coding and conclusions in a published exchange; the undermining effect’s size and scope in workplaces remains debated. Compare R-cerasoli-2014-intrinsic, which finds intrinsic motivation and incentives jointly predict performance.
generalizability: Moderate for leaders: the mechanism (controlling vs. informational rewards) transfers well; the effect size from lab play sessions should not be imported into compensation design.
relevance: The core evidence behind “rewards can backfire” — and the conditions that claim needs. Essential before designing recognition or bonus systems for people who already care about their craft.

title: Intrinsic Motivation and Extrinsic Incentives Jointly Predict Performance: A 40-Year Meta-Analysis
license: Copyright holder's terms. Linked, not reproduced.

verified.evidence: Title, authors, journal, volume, issue, pages, year and DOI matched on pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov (PMID 24491020); abstract findings (k = 183, N = 212,468; ρ = .21–.45; salience moderation) matched in indexed abstracts.

summary: A meta-analysis across school, work and physical domains asking whether intrinsic motivation and extrinsic incentives compete or work together in predicting performance. Intrinsic motivation was a medium-to-strong predictor of performance and stayed predictive when incentives were present. How tightly incentives were tied to performance mattered: intrinsic motivation was less important to performance when incentives were directly tied to it, and more important when incentives were indirect.
arguments: Intrinsic motivation predicts performance (ρ = .21–.45 across 183 samples, N = 212,468).
Incentives and intrinsic motivation are not simply opposed; both predict performance.
Incentive salience moderates the relation: directly performance-contingent incentives reduce the predictive importance of intrinsic motivation.
The authors report that intrinsic motivation relates more to the quality of performance and incentives more to its quantity.
design: Meta-analysis of 183 independent samples (N = 212,468) from school, work and physical domains spanning about forty years.
strengths: Broad, field-heavy synthesis that measures performance, not only free-choice play; tests moderators relevant to managers.
limitations: Much of the evidence is correlational, so intrinsic motivation and performance may share causes; heterogeneity across domains is large. The quality-versus-quantity pattern is reported by the authors but should be checked in the full text before relying on specific variance figures.
contested: Partly reconciles the Deci–Cameron debate rather than settling it; see R-deci-1999-meta.
generalizability: Good for organizational settings, which make up a large part of the sample; sport-specific evidence is thinner.
relevance: Replaces the slogan “money kills motivation” with a design question: which part of the work should carry a direct incentive, and which part depends on people caring?

title: When and Why Incentives (Don’t) Work to Modify Behavior
license: Free to read from the American Economic Association. Copyright holder’s terms. Linked, not reproduced.

verified.evidence: Title, authors, journal, volume, issue, pages, year and DOI matched on econpapers.repec.org and econbiz.de. Open access is from the AEA’s public JEP archive (not separately re-checked this session).

summary: A readable review of field and laboratory evidence on when monetary incentives change behavior in the intended direction. The authors argue that incentives have a direct price effect but also change how people interpret a task and what their behavior signals to others and to themselves, so incentives can raise effort in the short run while weakening intrinsic or social motives. They examine education, contributions to public goods, and lifestyle change such as smoking and exercise.
arguments: Incentives have a standard price effect and a psychological effect; the second can work against the first.
Paying for a behavior can change its meaning (from a social obligation to a market exchange), as in the authors’ discussion of fines for late pickup at day-care centers.
Short-run gains under incentives may not persist after incentives are removed, and can crowd out later voluntary engagement.
Design lessons: size, framing, timing and what the incentive signals all matter.
design: Narrative review of field experiments and laboratory studies in economics and psychology.
strengths: Written for non-specialists; draws on field experiments; balanced about when incentives do work.
limitations: A narrative review, not a meta-analysis; selection of studies reflects the authors’ program of research.
contested: Crowding-out is well documented in some settings and absent in others; see R-cerasoli-2014-intrinsic for a quantitative synthesis.
generalizability: High for public policy, education and health; reasonable for workplaces, where pay is already expected.
relevance: The best single entry point into the economics of incentives with behavioral caveats — the vocabulary this week’s exercise and assignment use.

summary: The standard short statement of self-determination theory. It proposes three basic psychological needs — autonomy, competence and relatedness — and a continuum of motivation from amotivation through externally controlled forms to internalized and intrinsic forms. Social environments that support the three needs are argued to foster internalization, persistence and well-being.
arguments: Motivation varies in kind (autonomous vs. controlled), not only in amount.
Autonomy, competence and relatedness are proposed as universal psychological needs.
Extrinsic motivation can be internalized (identified, integrated regulation) when the context supports the three needs.
design: Theoretical review summarizing a research program.
strengths: Clear, influential framework with a large empirical literature behind it.
limitations: Written by the theory’s founders; summarizes supportive evidence. The universality of the needs and the measurement of the regulation continuum are debated.
generalizability: Widely applied to work, education, health and sport; the distinctions are useful for leaders even where effect sizes vary.
relevance: Gives you the vocabulary — autonomy, competence, relatedness, internalization — for diagnosing why the same incentive energizes one group and alienates another.

summary: A foundational model of incentives when an agent divides effort among several tasks that differ in how well they can be measured. Strong incentives on the measurable task pull effort away from the hard-to-measure ones, so the optimal contract may use weak incentives, fixed pay, or a redesign of the job itself. The paper explains why many real jobs pay salaries rather than piece rates.
arguments: When tasks compete for the agent’s attention, incentive strength on one task must account for effort diverted from others.
If important tasks cannot be measured, low-powered incentives (salary) can be optimal.
Job design — grouping tasks by measurability — and ownership of assets are incentive instruments too.
strengths: Rigorous and general; explains a wide range of observed practices (teacher pay, salaried employees, restrictions on outside activities).
limitations: A model, not an empirical test; assumes agents respond rationally to the contract and ignores intrinsic motivation and norms.
generalizability: High: the multitask logic applies to any role mixing measured output with unmeasured quality, cooperation or development.
relevance: The single most useful model for anyone who designs metrics for coaches, analysts or managers whose most important work is hard to count.

summary: A classic essay collecting examples from politics, war, medicine, universities, sport and business in which organizations reward one behavior while hoping for another. Kerr argues the cause is usually an overreliance on objective, easily counted criteria and a reluctance to reward hard-to-observe behavior, and that fixing it begins by asking what the system actually pays for.
arguments: Organizations frequently reward behaviors they are trying to discourage and fail to reward those they want.
Misalignment arises from fascination with objective criteria, emphasis on visible behavior, and hypocrisy about stated goals.
People are better predicted by what is rewarded than by what is announced.
design: Conceptual essay built on illustrative cases.
limitations: Illustrative cases rather than systematic evidence; some examples are dated.
generalizability: High as a diagnostic heuristic; it identifies where to look, not how large the effect will be.
relevance: A short read that trains the reflex this week builds: before asking whether people are lazy or disloyal, ask what the system pays them for.

summary: The federal regulator’s announcement of its enforcement action against Wells Fargo Bank. The bureau stated that bank employees, working under sales targets and incentive-compensation programs, had opened deposit and credit-card accounts without customers’ knowledge or consent, and it imposed a $100 million penalty alongside a consent order requiring remediation.
arguments: Regulators linked unauthorized account openings to sales goals and incentive compensation.
The consent order required refunds to customers and changes to sales practices.
The case became a reference example of metric gaming at scale inside a large organization.
strengths: Primary regulatory source; establishes what a public authority found and ordered.
limitations: A press release summarizes a consent order; it does not establish the internal decision processes in detail, and the bank’s own account and later investigations add context not covered here.
generalizability: High as an illustration of how volume targets plus weak monitoring produce gaming; it is one organization and should not be over-generalized.
relevance: A concrete, documented example of what happens when an organization rewards counted outputs it cannot verify.

title: Estimating the Reproducibility of Psychological Science

verified.method: prior-knowledge (web-search budget exhausted before this record could be searched)
verified.evidence: Not confirmed by search in this session. Expected: Science 349(6251), aac4716 (August 2015), DOI 10.1126/science.aac4716; the project materials are public on the Open Science Framework. Recorded from the writer's prior knowledge of a widely cited work; title, authors, year, venue and DOI must be confirmed before publication.

summary: A large collaboration repeated 100 studies published in three prominent psychology journals, using high-powered designs and materials from the original authors where possible. Far fewer replications than originals produced statistically significant results, and replication effect sizes were on average about half the original estimates. Social psychology studies replicated less often than cognitive psychology studies.
arguments: Most original studies reported significant results; roughly a third or so of replications did.
Replication effects were, on average, about half the size of the originals.
Original effects that were larger and more strongly significant were more likely to replicate.
Replication rates differed by subfield, with social psychology lower than cognitive psychology.
design: Coordinated replication of 100 published studies by many independent teams.
strengths: Systematic sampling from journals rather than hand-picked targets; open materials.
limitations: One replication per study; some replications differed from originals in population or procedure; what counts as a successful replication is itself debated.
contested: Critics argued that differences in samples and procedures depress replication rates; the authors and later many-lab projects responded. The broad conclusion — many published effects are smaller or less reliable than reported — has held.
generalizability: Directly relevant to how much weight to give any single classic study cited in management or coaching.
relevance: Calibrates your trust in the famous studies that leadership books lean on.

summary: A registered replication report in which more than twenty laboratories ran the same preregistered protocol testing whether an initial act of self-control impairs performance on a later self-control task. The pooled effect was close to zero, in contrast to the sizable effects summarized in earlier meta-analyses of the ego-depletion literature.
arguments: A preregistered, multi-site test found an ego-depletion effect near zero.
Earlier meta-analytic estimates were likely inflated by publication bias and flexible analysis.
The result does not prove self-control never fatigues; it shows the standard laboratory paradigm did not reproduce the effect.
design: Preregistered multi-laboratory replication using a common randomized protocol.
strengths: Preregistration, many labs and large pooled sample remove most of the flexibility that inflated earlier estimates.
limitations: Tested one paradigm chosen in consultation with proponents; defenders argued the manipulation was too weak.
contested: Proponents dispute the protocol choice; later multisite tests have also found small or null effects. The popular “willpower is a muscle that runs out” claim should be treated as unsupported.
generalizability: Cautions against designing schedules or policies on the assumption that self-control is a depletable resource.
relevance: A model case of a once-famous finding that did not survive a rigorous test — a template for how to read the next one.

summary: A meta-analysis of studies that used Asch’s line-judgment task, in which a participant faces a unanimous group giving a clearly wrong answer. Conformity was a robust phenomenon, but its size varied: it was larger with larger majorities and in more collectivist cultures, and in U.S. studies it declined over the decades after Asch’s original work.
arguments: Conformity to a unanimous majority is a replicated phenomenon.
Its magnitude depends on group size, the participant’s relationship to the group and culture.
Conformity levels in U.S. samples declined over time, suggesting historical context matters.
design: Meta-analysis of Asch-paradigm studies conducted in many countries.
strengths: Quantifies a classic finding across time and cultures rather than relying on one iconic study.
limitations: Laboratory task with unambiguous stimuli and strangers; conformity in real organizations involves ambiguity, status and consequences.
generalizability: The direction (people shift toward unanimous groups) generalizes well; the specific rates do not.
relevance: Shows what a robust classic finding looks like when examined carefully: real, but variable and context-dependent.

summary: A review of experimental evidence that many people are conditionally cooperative: they reward kind actions and punish unkind ones even at a cost to themselves. The authors show how reciprocity can make incomplete contracts work (generous wages met with higher effort in gift-exchange experiments), how cooperation in public-goods games unravels without sanctions and is sustained when free riders can be punished, and how explicit incentives can interact with reciprocal motives.
arguments: A substantial share of people behave reciprocally, alongside a share who act selfishly.
Reciprocity helps enforce contracts and norms that cannot be written down fully.
Cooperation in groups tends to decay without the possibility of punishing free riders and can be sustained with it.
Explicit incentives perceived as hostile or distrustful can reduce reciprocal effort.
design: Review of laboratory and some field experiments.
strengths: Clear, influential, grounded in incentivized experiments.
limitations: Mostly laboratory games with modest stakes; the share of reciprocal types varies by population and setting.
contested: Field gift-exchange effects are often smaller or fade over time compared with laboratory results.
generalizability: Good for understanding norms, fairness and cooperation in teams; magnitudes from games should not be transferred directly.
relevance: Explains why fairness and perceived intent can matter as much as the size of a reward — and why a team can tolerate one free rider but not five.

title: Psychological Safety: A Meta-Analytic Review and Extension
license: Copyright holder's terms. Linked, not reproduced.

verified.method: web-search (by the Week 5 writer in this build; cross-checked against that record)
verified.evidence: Not searched by this writer (search budget exhausted). The identical record in sources/w05.json reports title, five authors, journal, volume 70 issue 1, pages 113–165 and DOI matched on econbiz.de, zendy.io and university repositories; every field here matches that record.

summary: A meta-analysis of the psychological safety literature — the shared belief that it is safe to take interpersonal risks such as asking questions or admitting errors. Psychological safety was associated with information sharing, learning behavior, engagement and performance, and was itself associated with supportive leadership and work design. Most of the underlying studies are correlational.
arguments: Psychological safety correlates positively with learning behavior, engagement and task performance.
Supportive leadership, peer support and work design characteristics are associated with higher psychological safety.
The construct operates at individual, team and organizational levels.
design: Meta-analysis of primarily cross-sectional field studies.
strengths: Aggregates a large field literature; examines antecedents and outcomes together.
limitations: Primary studies are mostly cross-sectional and often single-source, so causal direction and common-method bias are real concerns.
contested: Causal claims (“building psychological safety raises performance”) rest on thinner experimental and longitudinal evidence than popular accounts suggest.
generalizability: Relevant to any team that depends on speaking up about errors; sport-specific evidence is limited.
relevance: Separates the evidence on psychological safety from the slogan, so you can use the idea without overselling it.
